I don't really think that's the case. People like you and I are the early adopters. We never really were anyone's target demographic, and we never will be. If there's one thing I have faith in, is human's innate sense of curiosity. The more of us spread the word, the more it grows, organically. There's a reason people call it "going viral". Stuff usually flies under the radar for a very long time before it blows up or fizzles out; but the stuff that is truly worth it, that is innovative, will stick around and grow until those further and further out of the loop pick up on it.

The majority of people don't care about this stuff, and really: never have. Since before the internet, even. When a newspaper would become heavily censored or edited for content by a government, people would just start up their own, until it too became a cog in the system, which would in turn spawn another. Lather, rinse, repeat. Hell, the people that started the original dial-up BBSs, or those who first frequented Usenet weren't "the majority". They were the very definition of 'fringe': the nerds and social outcasts that had nothing better to do with their time than tinker around with this "weird, new technology that no one understands". Computers were considered toys for geeks not too long ago.

Look at linux. When it was first posted to a Usenet group back in 1991, it was a pet project. Even Linus himself didn't think it would ever become anything other than a curiosity,
